To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
abomasal glucose administration to dairy cows in early lactation increases portal glucose supply without affecting the hepatic gluconeogenic capacity.

abomasal glucose supplementation to periparturiant dairy cows in very-early lactation (i) increased portal-drained visceral glucose uptake, (ii) decreased net hepatic glucose production, (iii) decreased whole-body glucose recycling via lactate, (iv) decreased feed intake and milk yield, (v) decreased the concentrations of plasma glucose, insulin, and beta-hydroxy-butyrate, and (vi) increased the concentration of plasma nonesterified fatty acid.
the net portal flux of abomasally infused glucose increased by 67%, whereas the net hepatic glucose flux was not affected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of abomassal glucose infusion on the splanchnic uptake and release of glucose and on the whole-body glucose supply and demand in dairy cows in early lactation.
the effects of abomassal glucose infusion on the glucose metabolism in dairy cows in early lactation.
the effect of abomasal infusion of glucose on glucose metabolism in peripartrient dairy cows.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
abomasal glucose supplementation in early lactation improves glucose availability to the peripheral tissues, but the overall effect of this treatment is negative, because the milk yield is decreased.

glucose infusion to periparturition dairy cows improves the metabolic status of these animals by reducing their negative energy balance and increasing the availability of glucose for peripheral tissues.

glucose infused in the abomasum of dairy cows in the early postpartum period was used as a source of energy for the splanchnic tissues and the peripheral tissues and that the infused glucose was not used for hepatic gluconeogenic purposes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glucose is a good energy source for the small intestine and that the Cori cycle is an inefficient way of supplying the periphery with energy in early lactation.
the abomasal glucose supply was a very efficient source of glucose for the peripheral tissues of the dairy cow in early lactation.

glucose infusion in the periparturition period improved the glucogenic status of cows in very early postpartum period and that the improved glucogenic status was beneficial for the cow, but not for milk production.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the abomasal infusion of glucose in early lactation improved glucose supply to the periphery and decreased the dependence on the Cori cycle, but it also impaired metabolic adaptations to early lactation.
the small intestinal glucose absorption can be used to increase whole-body glucose availability in peripartum cows.

abomasal glucose supplementation to periparturients is a useful tool to study the regulation of splanchnic glucose metabolism and to study the effects on glucose metabolism of other nutrients that are infused in the abomasum.
